<p class="print-note">Eight survey items, each broken in a different way — and
every one of them has appeared in a real study. Cut along the dashed lines,
deal one per team. Page&nbsp;2 is the critique sheet and the sample-size box.</p>

<div class="sheetwrap">
<div class="cards">

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 1</span>
    <h3>The compliment</h3>
    <p class="q">"How much did you enjoy our improved checkout experience?"</p>
    <p class="opts">A great deal · Quite a lot · Somewhat · A little</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>Two things are wrong.</b> Name both, then rewrite it.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 2</span>
    <h3>Two questions in a coat</h3>
    <p class="q">"Was the product affordable and easy to use?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Yes · No</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>What does "no" mean here?</b> Rewrite it.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 3</span>
    <h3>No way to disagree</h3>
    <p class="q">"How would you rate our customer service?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Excellent · Very good · Good · Fair</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>What will the average look like, and why?</b> Rewrite it.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 4</span>
    <h3>Often, compared to what?</h3>
    <p class="q">"How often do you buy organic produce?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Often · Sometimes · Rarely · Never</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>Two respondents answer "sometimes."</b> Do they mean the same thing?</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 5</span>
    <h3>The right answer is obvious</h3>
    <p class="q">"Do you consider environmental impact when deciding what to buy?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Always · Usually · Sometimes · Never</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>Why will this overstate?</b> How would you design around it?</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 6</span>
    <h3>Assumes the answer</h3>
    <p class="q">"Where do you usually buy your protein powder?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Supermarket · Online · Specialist shop · Gym</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>Who cannot answer this?</b> What does that do to your sample?</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 7</span>
    <h3>The free promise</h3>
    <p class="q">"Would you pay $2 more for a sustainably sourced version?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Yes · No</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>This one has a name.</b> What would you do instead?</p>
  </div>

  <div class="card">
    <span class="n">Card 8</span>
    <h3>A lot</h3>
    <p class="q">"Do you spend a lot on groceries each week?"</p>
    <p class="opts">Yes · No</p>
    <p class="ask"><b>What number would you rather have?</b> Rewrite it.</p>
  </div>

</div>

<div class="defence">
  <h3>Critique sheet — team <span style="color:#b31b1b">______</span> &nbsp;·&nbsp; card <span style="color:#b31b1b">____</span></h3>

  <p class="lbl">How this runs</p>
  <p class="vocab" style="font-style:normal">Every team works its card at the
  same time. Then <b>one team is drawn at random</b> to present while the room
  attacks — and we draw again. <b>Points for an attack that lands</b>, and you
  must name the flaw, not just dislike the wording.</p>

  <p class="vocab">Name it: <b>leading</b> · <b>double-barrelled</b> ·
  <b>unbalanced scale</b> · <b>vague quantifier</b> ·
  <b>social desirability</b> · <b>assumes the behaviour</b> ·
  <b>hypothetical bias</b> · <b>no reference period</b></p>

  <p class="lbl">The flaw, named</p>
  <div class="row"></div>

  <p class="lbl">Our rewrite</p>
  <div class="row"></div>
  <div class="row"></div>

  <p class="lbl">What an answer to the rewritten item actually lets you conclude</p>
  <div class="row"></div>

  <div class="power">
    <h4>Then: how many people do you need?</h4>
    <p>You cannot decide that from ambition. It falls out of two numbers —
    how noisy the outcome is (σ), and the smallest difference worth
    caring about (d).</p>
    <p class="eq"><b>n per group ≈ 16 σ² / d²</b></p>
    <p>Read it backwards and it is more useful. With <i>n</i> per group, the
    smallest effect you could reliably detect is</p>
    <p class="eq"><b>MDE ≈ 4 σ / √n</b></p>
    <p><b>Quadrupling the sample only halves the detectable effect.</b>
    Precision is expensive, which is why this is a design decision and not
    an afterthought.</p>
    <p><b>The question that matters:</b> with the sample you can actually
    afford, is the smallest effect you could detect still interesting? If
    not, do not run it — that is meeting 3's "no significant effect, kill
    the programme" card, seen a month before it happens to you.</p>
    <p class="lbl" style="margin-top:0.14in">Our σ, our d, our n — and is the MDE interesting?</p>
    <div class="row"></div>
  </div>
</div>
</div>
